name: Armitage Bridge
text: Your train passes near Armitage Bridge, on the train's {side}, a village straddling the River Holme. It is dominated by the old woollen mill of John Brooke and Sons, said to be the oldest family business in the country, founded in 1541; the mill is now an office park.

name: Honley High School
text: Your train passes near Honley High School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1932 as Holme Valley Grammar School, with room for 480 pupils and 14 teachers. It became a comprehensive and took its present name in 1973, and now has around 1,250 pupils aged 11 to 16.

name: Church of St Thomas, Thurstonland
text: Your train passes near the Church of St Thomas, Thurstonland, on the train's {side}, an Arts and Crafts church in the Gothic Revival style, finished in 1870. It was paid for by the fifth Earl of Dartmouth, and its nave has an arch-braced hammerbeam roof.

name: Thunder Bridge
text: Your train passes near Thunder Bridge, on the train's {side}, a hamlet and conservation area with a Grade II listed road bridge over Shepley Dike. It was once also known as Founder Bridge.

name: Lower Cumberworth
text: Your train passes near Lower Cumberworth, on the train's {side}, a village of around 200 homes. Its name comes from the Old English Cumbreworð, meaning "Cumbre's enclosure" or "the enclosure of the Cumbrians".

name: Denby Dale Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Denby Dale Viaduct, which curves over the Dearne valley. The first viaduct here was built of timber because a stonemasons' strike had made stone too costly, and was blown down in a gale in January 1847; the present stone one replaced its timber successor in 1880.

name: Penistone Paramount Cinema
text: Your train passes near the Paramount Cinema, on the train's {side}, opened in 1914 as the town's assembly hall and showing silent films from 1915. Its Compton organ was built in 1937 for the Paramount Theatre in Birmingham; a local trust bought it in 2000, and the cinema was renamed in its honour.

name: Silkstone Common
text: Your train passes Silkstone Common, on the train's {side}. In 1877 the South Yorkshire Coal and Iron Company built the South Yorkshire Buildings here, planned housing laid out in a regular pattern among small allotment gardens, unlike the terraces strung out along the village's older roads.

name: Penny Pie Park
text: Your train passes Penny Pie Park, on the train's {side}, an old landfill site that is now a playing field and park, ringed by the A628. Pigeon fanciers race pigeons from it, hot air balloons and air ambulances land on it, and it hosts the Barnsley Mini Olympics each summer.

name: All Saints Church, Darton
text: Your train passes near All Saints Church, Darton, on the train's {side}. A church stood here by 1150; the friars of Monk Bretton Priory, granted the living by Richard III in 1483, replaced the Norman church with the present one in the Perpendicular style, finished in 1517.

name: Chantry Chapel of St Mary the Virgin, Wakefield
text: Your train passes near the Chantry Chapel of St Mary the Virgin, on the train's {side}, on the medieval bridge over the River Calder. Licensed in 1356, it is the only survivor of Wakefield's four chantry chapels, and the oldest and most ornate of England's surviving bridge chapels.

name: St Peter and St Leonard's Church, Horbury
text: Your train passes near St Peter and St Leonard's Church, Horbury, on the train's {side}. The architect John Carr, the son of a Horbury stonemason, offered to build it at his own expense; it was finished in 1794, and is listed Grade I.

name: Thornhill power station
text: Your train passes near Thornhill power station, on the train's {side}, beside the River Calder. Coal-fired electricity was made here from 1902 until 1982, the coal arriving by rail, and a gas turbine power station opened on the site in 1998.

name: Ledgard Bridge
text: Your train passes near Ledgard Bridge, on the train's {side}, over the River Calder. The first bridge here was a wooden one of 1303; the present one, built in 1800, survived the great flood of September 1946.

name: Dewsbury Minster
text: Your train passes near Dewsbury Minster, on the train's {side}, the parish church of All Saints, dating from the 13th century. Each Christmas Eve its bell, Black Tom, tolls once for every year since Christ's birth: the "Devil's Knell", a tradition dating from the 15th century.

name: Batley Variety Club
text: Your train passes near the old Batley Variety Club, on the train's {side}, opened in 1967 on a disused sewage site by James and Betty Corrigan after a trip to Las Vegas. Louis Armstrong, Shirley Bassey, Roy Orbison and Morecambe and Wise all played here, and at its peak it had 300,000 members.

name: Howley Hall
text: Your train passes near the ruins of Howley Hall, on the train's {side}, an Elizabethan country house built for Sir John Savile between about 1585 and 1590. There was fighting here in the Civil War in 1643, and the hall was pulled down between 1717 and 1730; it is now a scheduled monument.

name: White Rose Centre
text: Your train passes near the White Rose Centre, on the train's {side}, a shopping centre opened in 1997 on the site of the old Morley sewage works. Building it meant sealing disused mine shafts and moving 750,000 cubic metres of soil; it is named after the White Rose of York.

name: Temple Works
text: Your train passes near Temple Works, on the train's {side}, a flax mill built for John Marshall between 1836 and 1840 in the Egyptian style, its front based on temples at Antaeopolis and Edfu. It was said to be the biggest single room in the world, and sheep grazed on its grass roof, which kept the air inside humid for the flax.

name: Armley Mills
text: Your train passes near Armley Mills, on the train's {side}, once the world's largest woollen mill, built by Benjamin Gott in 1805 between the Leeds and Liverpool Canal and the River Aire. It closed as a mill in 1969 and is now the Leeds Industrial Museum.

name: Headingley Stadium
text: Your train passes near Headingley Stadium, on the train's {side}, where Yorkshire's cricket ground and the Leeds Rhinos' rugby league ground are joined by a shared stand. The cricket ground opened in 1891 and has held Test matches since 1899.

name: Abbey House Museum
text: Your train passes near Abbey House Museum, on the train's {side}, in the inner gatehouse of Kirkstall Abbey. After the abbey was dissolved it became a farmhouse; since 1927 it has been a museum, with recreated Victorian streets of shops on its ground floor.

name: Arthington Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Arthington Viaduct over the River Wharfe: 21 sandstone arches built between 1845 and 1849 for the Leeds and Thirsk Railway. It stands on the boundary between West and North Yorkshire, and is listed in both.

name: St Robert's Church, Pannal
text: Your train passes near St Robert's Church, on the train's {side}, whose crenellated tower is a local landmark. A wooden church here was rebuilt in sandstone in the 14th century by Trinitarian friars from Knaresborough Priory, perhaps when it was rededicated to St Robert of Knaresborough.

name: Crimple Valley Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Crimple Valley Viaduct, 31 arches over Crimple Beck, finished in 1848 for the York and North Midland Railway and listed Grade II*. Another railway, the Leeds Northern, once ran beneath one of its arches.

name: Tewit Well
text: Your train passes near Tewit Well, on the train's {side}, on the edge of the Stray: the first iron-rich spring found in the town. In 1571 William Slingsby found its water was like that at Spa in Belgium, and named it after a local word for the lapwing; the stone cover over it was moved here in 1842 from the Old Sulphur Well.

name: Grove House, Harrogate
text: Your train passes near Grove House, on the train's {side}, built in the 18th century as the World's End Inn. The inventor Samson Fox bought it in 1882 and lit it with water gas he made in his basement laboratory; he also paid for the Royal College of Music's new building.

name: Mother Shipton's Cave
text: Your train passes near Mother Shipton's Cave, on the train's {side}, by the River Nidd, where the legendary prophetess is said to have been born. Its petrifying well, whose water crusts over things left in it, has been shown to paying visitors since 1630, making it England's oldest tourist attraction to charge a fee.

name: Knaresborough Castle
text: Your train passes near Knaresborough Castle, on the train's {side}, a ruined fortress on a cliff above the River Nidd. Edward II gave it to Piers Gaveston, and Queen Philippa of Hainault often spent summers here; Parliament had it dismantled in 1648, and many buildings in the town are made of "castle stone".

name: St John the Baptist Church, Kirk Hammerton
text: Your train passes near St John the Baptist Church, Kirk Hammerton, on the train's {side}. Its Anglo-Saxon tower was added around 950, and the older Saxon church, now its south aisle, was built largely of stone taken from the ruins of Roman York.

name: Wilstrop
text: Your train passes near Wilstrop, on the train's {side}, a parish of about 60 people with no modern village. Its medieval village was emptied in the 15th century, when the landowner evicted the villagers to make way for sheep; earthworks of it survive near the River Nidd.

name: National Railway Museum
text: Your train passes near the National Railway Museum, on the train's {side}, on the site of the old York North engine shed since 1975. It holds the national collection, including Mallard and a Japanese bullet train, and is the largest museum of its kind in Britain.

name: St Everilda's Church, Nether Poppleton
text: Your train passes near St Everilda's Church, Nether Poppleton, on the train's {side}, one of only two churches in the country dedicated to Everilda, an Anglo-Saxon saint. A church stood here by 1088; much of its 12th-century rebuilding survives, and its altar of 1939 was carved by Robert Thompson.

name: Otterington Hall
text: Your train passes near Otterington Hall, on the train's {side}, a Grade II listed mansion in South Otterington. The Furness family planted much of its topiary garden from the 1920s, called one of the best in England and certainly the best in Yorkshire.

name: Croft Bridge
text: Your train passes near Croft Bridge, on the train's {side}, a medieval bridge of seven arches over the River Tees between County Durham and North Yorkshire. Each new Bishop of Durham is greeted here with the falchion that legend says killed the Sockburn Worm, a ceremony revived in 1973.

name: St Thomas' Church, Brompton
text: Your train passes near St Thomas' Church, Brompton, on the train's {side}, parts of which date from about 1180. Inside are three hogback tombstones from the early 10th century, and the church is listed Grade I.

name: Bar Convent
text: Your train passes near the Bar Convent, on the train's {side}, by Micklegate Bar. Founded in 1686, when Catholic convents were against the law, it was run in secret, and it is the oldest surviving Catholic convent in the British Isles; it now has a museum and a café.

name: St Mary the Virgin's Church, Church Fenton
text: Your train passes near St Mary the Virgin's Church, on the train's {side}, a particularly small cruciform church whose oldest parts date from about 1230. Its tower carries warning lights for aircraft using the nearby Leeds East Airport.

name: Barkston Ash
text: Your train passes near Barkston Ash, on the train's {side}, a village of about 370 people. The "Ash" in its name comes from a large ash tree said to stand near the centre of the old county of Yorkshire, where meetings of the wapentake were held; the parish took the full name only in 1976.

name: Roman Road station
text: Your train passes the site of Roman Road station, on the train's {side}, one of the shortest-lived stations in the United Kingdom. It opened with the Leeds and Selby Railway on September 22nd 1834 and closed on November 10th, less than two months later.
